newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban fends off attacks, holds on to Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban fends off attacks, holds on to Kabul.

text.p: The puritanical Islamic Taleban seem to be strengthening their grip on Kabul and its surroundings despite numerous attacks by the opposition.
When the Taleban first took Kabul in late September, many Afghan watchers predicted that the forces of the ousted government would counter attack and dislodge the city's new rulers.

A counter attack by the opposition in mid-October did push the Taleban south from their positions of furthest advance to within 20 km (15 miles) of Kabul, but despite numerous attacks since then the opposition have not only failed to make any significant advances but have actually lost some ground.
Afghan watchers say that a factor hindering the opposition is the inherent weaknesses that exist in their alliance.

The opposition alliance consists of the forces of the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani under his top military commander Ahmed Shah Masood, and those of the northern leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum. The alliance was created shortly after Kabul fell to the Taleban in late September.
Dostum and the now ex-government have been allies before. Dostum is a former communist general whose defection in April 1992 brought about the downfall of the communist regime.
He allied himself with Masood who held most of Kabul after the defeat of the communists. But in January 1994, Dostum switched sides and started fighting Masood.

"The opposition alliance is riven by distrust that dates from the split in 1994." said one Afghan watcher in Kabul. "They are spending as much time protecting themselves against their allies as they are fighting the Taleban."

The analyst, who preferred to remain anonymous, said the opposition also have logistical problems. "Masood has all of his arms and ammunition tied up in the Panjsheer valley and he can't get them to the front line." he said. "Dostum has kept control of much of the equipment he has supplied and his men are not as committed as Masood's."
Masood is from the Panjsheer valley and used it as a base during the 13-year war against the communists.

When the Taleban moved rapidly north after taking Kabul he retreated into the valley with most of his heavy weapons and destroyed the road to prevent the Taleban following. The road has not yet been repaired and most of his weapons are still stuck in the valley.

The Taleban are also benefitting from the high morale of their troops. Many of them are young men untainted by the cynicism that had crept into the ranks of the fighters involved in the four years of interneicine carnage in and around Kabul. They maintain their belief in the justice and ultimate victory of their cause.

Many people expected a violent reaction after the fall of Kabul from the city's relatively cosmopolitan population against the strict interpretation of Islam advocated by the Taleban. It has not appeared.

"The Kabulis are not happy with the Taleban, but they are not willing to die for the alternative." says the analyst. "Rabbani's regime is remembered for food and fuel blockades, corruption and the lack of security. When Dostum was in Kabul in 1994, his men were renowned for their lawlessness; there is no way the Kabulis want them back."
"The people of the city have lost hope in all of the factions, now they just want to be left alone to survive." he said.
The Taleban control 75 per cent of Afghanistan, including all but one of the crucial major cross-border supply routes.

Masood and his forces in the Panjsheer rely on the all-weather road over the Hindu Kush at the Salang Pass some 120 kilometers (75 miles) north of Kabul. If the Taleban can take the Salang Pass, Masood will be trapped in the Panjsheer with no way of gettnng further supplies until the other passes clear of snow after the winter.
The United Nations Special Mission to Afghanistan is trying to find a mutually acceptable formula to halt the fighting, but have so far had little success.

"Neither side has shown a willingness to make the compromises that will be essential for any lasting peace in Afghanistan. While they talk about a negotiated solution their actions show a belief in a military solution. Until this changes, I can see little chance of peace coming to Afghanistan." says the analyst.
